analysis.investment_thesis: Apollo Micro Systems is a small Indian defense electronics firm riding genuine Atmanirbhar Bharat tailwinds, but at 113x trailing P/E with a 10% ROE and chronically negative free cash flow, investors are paying a spectacular price for a mediocre business. I don't pay 113 times earnings for a company that hasn't generated meaningful free cash in four of five years.
key_strengths: Genuine defense sector tailwinds: India's indigenization push (Atmanirbhar Bharat) provides a structural long runway for domestic defense electronics suppliers.
Solid revenue and profit trajectory: revenue 5Y CAGR of 18%, net profit CAGR of 32% — growth is real, not illusory.
Manageable leverage: Debt/Equity of 0.33 is within acceptable limits, and the 2025 equity raise (reserves jumped from 490 to 1,046 Cr) has shored up the balance sheet.
key_risks: Chronic free cash flow destruction: FCF was negative in 4 of 5 years (-16, -50, -131, -82 Cr), meaning reported profits are largely paper — working capital and capex devour every rupee earned.
ROE of 10% is well below my 15% threshold and completely inconsistent with a 113x P/E multiple — the market is pricing in a business quality that doesn't yet exist.
Finance costs growing at 17.8% CAGR (now 34 Cr vs. 56 Cr net profit) — interest consumes 61% of net earnings, making profitability fragile to any revenue slowdown.
red_flags: P/E of 113x on a 10% ROE business is indefensible — even at forward P/E of 65.8x, you need flawless execution for years just to break even.
Operating CF of just 10 Cr on 56 Cr reported net profit in FY2025 signals severe working capital deterioration — a hallmark of government defense contractors with long collection cycles.
Capex surging to 92 Cr in FY2025 (vs. 23 Cr in FY2022) while generating essentially no free cash flow — this is a capital-hungry business, not a compounder.
Equity dilution: reserves nearly doubled in one year (490→1,046 Cr) suggesting a large QIP/fundraise, meaning existing shareholders bore dilution to fund a cash-burning machine.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Apollo Micro Systems operates in the right sector — Indian defense electronics with government mandates to source domestically — and the revenue trajectory is encouraging at 18% CAGR. But the operating metrics tell a sobering story. ROE sits at a pedestrian 10%, well below the 15% minimum I require before even considering a purchase. Operating margins of 17.56% sound decent, but after finance costs that consumed 61% of FY2025 net profit, true economic earnings are thin. Critically, the free cash flow record is dismal: -16, -50, -131, and -82 Cr in the last four years. When a business reports 56 Cr in net profit but generates only 10 Cr in operating cash flow, I know working capital is swallowing the business — a chronic problem for defense suppliers dependent on slow-paying government customers.

The valuation borders on the absurd. At 113x trailing earnings and 58.6x EV/EBITDA, this stock is priced as though it is a near-monopoly compounder with decades of visible earnings at 25%+ ROE. It is neither. A wonderful business at a fair price this is not — it is a fair business at a wonderful price for the seller. The defense sector story is genuine, but story and reality must be distinguished. I would need to see sustained ROE above 15%, consistent free cash generation, and a P/E below 30x before this would warrant even a second look.
